To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk of developing alcohol abuse/dependence among offspring increases with increasing age among Whites but decreases with increasing age among Blacks.

familial alcoholism is a more potent risk factor for alcohol problems for whites than for blacks; that familial alcoholism has a stronger association with alcohol problems among younger than among older individuals; and that the association between familial alcoholism and alcohol problems is stronger for females than for men.
the risk of developing alcohol problems in offspring is influenced by familial alcohol problems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of sociodemographics on familial alcohol problems.
the development of alcoholism and other addictive disorders in offspring as a function of familial alcoholism and other risk factors.
the development of a comprehensive model for the study of familial alcohol problems in general populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
race, age, sex, SES, and family history of alcohol problems all influence risk of alcohol problems.

race, sex, and age do moderate the relationship between familial alcohol problems and alcohol abuse/dependence, and that the moderating effect of these variables is dependent on the specific sample being investigated.
the effect of family alcohol problems is moderated by race, age, sex, but not by socioeconomic status.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk associated with family history is greater in older white males, and that the risk associated is greater in older black males than in black females.
the influence of familial alcoholism on the development of offspring alcoholism is not uniform across the general population.
the risk of familial alcohol problems is higher among whites and that the effect of familial risk on offspring alcohol problems varies as a function of age and sex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
race, sex and age are important factors to take into consideration when investigating alcohol problems in families.
family history of alcohol problems is associated with a greater risk of alcohol problems in offspring, and that this risk is moderated by age, sex, race and, to a lesser extent, SES.
the risk associated with a positive parental history of alcohol problems is different for different racial and ethnic groups and that it may change with age and gender.
